blocks.text: How to reason it out

The correct choice is “A set of values seen so far.” The scan checks whether the current value is already in the seen set. If it is, a duplicate exists; otherwise the value is inserted before moving on. Exact counts are unnecessary because the contract asks only for a yes-or-no answer.
Presence state is sufficient when the result depends only on whether a value appeared before.

Only the immediately previous value. — A repeated value may be separated from its earlier occurrence in an unsorted input.
An output array containing every processed value. — Storing the processed prefix does not provide efficient membership state and retains unnecessary data.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The correct choice is “Map each value to its index only when that value is first encountered.” When a value is absent from the map, its current index becomes the first occurrence. Later occurrences must not overwrite that entry. A count alone does not preserve position.
The state update rule must preserve the first index rather than replace it.

The correct choice is “[7, 7]”. The first two copies are legal. The third and fourth exceed the maximum multiplicity and must be removed. Deduplication is not always equivalent to keeping exactly one copy.

blocks.text: First state the required count, order, and mutation guarantees. Inspect the candidate against those guarantees, then derive a minimal input from the suspected violation, and finally compare the produced output with the postcondition. For a candidate that sorts before deduplicating, a stable-first-occurrence contract exposes an order violation; [2, 1, 2] demonstrates the wrong [1, 2] instead of [2, 1].
